emblem: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="era-emblem" viewBox="0 0 120 120" fill="none" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="60" cy="60" r="54" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.35"/><g opacity="0.85" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1"><line x1="60" y1="26" x2="60" y2="34"/><line x1="44" y1="30" x2="48" y2="37"/><line x1="76" y1="30" x2="72" y2="37"/></g><path d="M60 50 C51 44 40 44 33 47 V82 C40 79 51 79 60 85" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><path d="M60 50 C69 44 80 44 87 47 V82 C80 79 69 79 60 85" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="60" y1="50" x2="60" y2="85" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.2"/></svg>

ch31.title: The Reformation
ch31.summary: The sixteenth-century revolt that split Western Christianity — begun as a quarrel over the sale of forgiveness, carried across a continent by the printing press, and ending in a hundred years of war. From Luther's Ninety-Five Theses and the five solas, through Calvin and the radical Anabaptists, the Catholic Counter-Reformation and Trent, to the Peace of Westphalia; with a symbology section on the printed vernacular Bible, iconoclasm, and the turn from image to word — keeping the theological claims as faith and flagging the door legend and the Weber thesis as debated.
ch31.plateCaption: A rose enclosing a heart and cross, after the seal Luther chose — the living faith of the believer at the center of a movement that put the Word above all. An original geometric rendering, not a facsimile of the seal.

ch32.title: The Witch Trials
ch32.summary: The two-and-a-half centuries in which early modern Europe hunted, tortured, and killed tens of thousands of its own people — overwhelmingly poor women — for a crime that, as imagined, did not exist. Told per the project's standard as documented persecution, not validation: the fabricated diabolical witch, the Malleus Maleficarum, torture and the chain-reaction panics, the gender and the regional exceptions, Salem, and the debunked Murray witch-cult myth — with a symbology section on the Devil's mark, the scripted confession, and the inverted sabbath.
ch32.plate: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="plate-art" viewBox="0 0 200 200" fill="none" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="92" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.3"/><g stroke="#e7c680" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="100" y1="44" x2="100" y2="150" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M78 158 L122 158 L112 150 L88 150 Z" stroke-width="1.4"/><circle cx="100" cy="44" r="3.4" fill="#e7c680"/><line x1="42" y1="60" x2="158" y2="80" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="42" y1="60" x2="42" y2="70" stroke-width="0.9"/><path d="M26 70 Q42 88 58 70" stroke-width="1.3"/><line x1="26" y1="70" x2="42" y2="60" stroke-width="0.7" opacity="0.6"/><line x1="58" y1="70" x2="42" y2="60" stroke-width="0.7" opacity="0.6"/><line x1="158" y1="80" x2="158" y2="100" stroke-width="0.9"/><path d="M142 100 Q158 118 174 100" stroke-width="1.3"/><line x1="142" y1="100" x2="158" y2="80" stroke-width="0.7" opacity="0.6"/><line x1="174" y1="100" x2="158" y2="80" stroke-width="0.7" opacity="0.6"/></g></svg>
ch32.plateCaption: The scales of justice, thrown out of balance — a persecution that wore the robes of law to punish an imaginary crime. An original figure, chosen to mark the trials as a miscarriage of justice, not to depict their victims.

ch33.title: African Traditional Religion
ch33.summary: The vast family of indigenous religions of sub-Saharan Africa — a Supreme God above intermediary spirits and living ancestors, read through divination and danced in masks — and how, in the slave-trade centuries, these faiths were carried across the Atlantic and survived hidden inside the saints of their captors. Yoruba orisha and Ifa, Fon vodun, Akan and Kongo; the Middle Passage and syncretism; a symbology section on Ifa's 256 binary odu, Adinkra, and Nsibidi — rejecting the colonial 'fetishism' labels and keeping the oral, mediated record honest.
ch33.plateCaption: An Ifa divination motif — the diviner’s marks that record one of the 256 odu, a sacred binary read from palm nuts. An original geometric rendering in the tradition’s idiom, not a specific tray.

ch34.title: Sikhism
ch34.summary: The faith born in the Punjab five centuries ago from the meeting of Hindu devotion and Muslim mysticism — one formless God (Ik Onkar), honest work, and radical equality. From Guru Nanak's 'there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' through the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib (which enshrines Hindu and Muslim saints), the Khalsa and the Five Ks; with a symbology section on Ik Onkar, the Khanda, and the Naam — keeping the Gurus' history distinct from the janamsakhi legend and handling the synthesis-vs-revelation question with care.
ch34.plate: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" class="plate-art" viewBox="0 0 200 200" fill="none" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="100" cy="100" r="92" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="0.3"/><circle cx="100" cy="104" r="40" stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="2.4"/><g stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" fill="none"><path d="M92 168 C 58 150 46 108 60 66"/><path d="M108 168 C 142 150 154 108 140 66"/></g><g stroke="#e7c680" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M100 26 L107 46 L104 150 L96 150 L93 46 Z" fill="#e7c680" opacity="0.15"/><path d="M100 26 L107 46 L104 150 L96 150 L93 46 Z"/><line x1="100" y1="30" x2="100" y2="150" stroke-width="0.7" opacity="0.6"/></g></svg>
ch34.plateCaption: The Khanda — the double-edged sword of divine truth within the chakkar of God’s oneness, flanked by the two kirpans of spiritual and temporal power. An original geometric rendering of the Sikh emblem.

ch63.title: Oceania
ch63.summary: Mana, taboo, and the gods of the sea — the religions of the Pacific, settled by the greatest voyage in human history. The two master-concepts of mana (sacred power) and tapu (the source of ‘taboo’) that ordered all of life; the Polynesian world-parents Rangi and Papa and the great gods (Tangaroa, Tane, Tu, Rongo) and the trickster-hero Maui; the sacred chief (ariki) and priest (tohunga), the marae, and human sacrifice; Rapa Nui’s moai as ancestor-images channeling mana and the later birdman cult of Makemake; Melanesia’s ancestor cults, masks, and secret societies; and the millenarian cargo cults (John Frum), logical within their own cosmology. A symbology of the moai and tiki, the tatau (origin of ‘tattoo’), and the star-path — with the contested Rapa Nui ‘collapse’ narrative and the condescending ‘cargo cult’ caricature both flagged.

ch63.plateCaption: Moai standing on their ahu, facing inland with their backs to the sea, beneath a path of stars such as Pacific navigators steered by. A schematic drawing, not a copy of particular statues.

v11.title: The Rohonc Codex
v11.held: Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Budapest
v11.summary: 448 small pages in an unknown script of about 200 signs, with crucifixions beside crescents. Given to the Hungarian Academy in 1838, it is suspected as a forger's hoax and proposed as a coded prayer book. Every reading so far, and why none has held.

v04.title: The Shroud of Turin
v04.dated: Radiocarbon 1260–1390 CE (1988; contested); documented from c. 1354
v04.held: Chapel of the Shroud, Turin Cathedral — owned by the Holy See since 1983
v04.summary: A 4.4-metre linen bearing the faint negative-like image of a crucified man — documented from the 1350s, radiocarbon-dated to 1260–1390, its image still unexplained. Every test and every challenge, set side by side, with the Church's own distinction between icon and relic.

v15.title: The True Cross
v15.held: Fragments worldwide: Rome, Jerusalem, Mount Athos, Paris and others
v15.summary: Wood venerated as the Cross in fourth-century Jerusalem, where deacons guarded it because a pilgrim once bit off a piece. Helena's discovery legend and Eusebius's silence, Calvin's 'shipload' and the 1870 attempt to measure every fragment.

v25.title: The Veil of Veronica
v25.dated: Venerated at St Peter's from the 12th century
v25.held: St Peter's Basilica, Rome; rival image at Manoppello
v25.summary: The 'true image' of Christ's face that drew the crowds of the 1300 Jubilee. A legend not in the Gospels, a name with a false etymology, a relic reported lost in the Sack of Rome yet still shown each year, and a transparent veil at Manoppello claimed to be the original.

v78.title: The Malleus Maleficarum
v78.dated: Written by the Dominican Heinrich Kramer (Institoris), first printed 1486
v78.held: Printed at Speyer in 1486 and reprinted many times; copies in many libraries
v78.summary: The 'Hammer of Witches', a Latin handbook on identifying, trying and punishing witches, written by the inquisitor Heinrich Kramer after a failed witch trial at Innsbruck. How much it was actually used in the trials, and how far Jacob Sprenger contributed, are both debated.

v88.title: The Skull of “Mary Magdalene” at Saint-Maximin
v88.dated: Venerated there since the “discovery” of 1279; the present gilded reliquary is dated MDCCCLX (1860)
v88.held: Crypt of the Basilica of Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, Provence, France
v88.summary: A darkened skull in a gilded reliquary of flowing golden hair carried by four angels, venerated as Mary Magdalene's since Charles of Salerno announced her tomb in 1279. The Provence legend has no trace before the eleventh century, Vézelay claimed her first, and a 2017 study reconstructed the face of a woman of about fifty without identifying her.

v64.title: The Benin Bronzes
v64.dated: Cast c. 13th–19th century; the palace plaques mostly 16th–17th century
v64.held: Dispersed since 1897: British Museum, Berlin, and more than 130 other institutions; returns to Nigeria under way since 2022
v64.summary: Thousands of cast brass plaques, heads and ivory carvings from the royal court of Benin, made for the altars of the Oba's ancestors and for the palace. The British army looted them in 1897 and sold them to museums around the world. Their return is one of the defining restitution cases of our time.

v77.title: The Haitian Vèvè
v77.dated: A living practice; documented from the 19th and 20th centuries
v77.held: Drawn anew for each ceremony and effaced during it; recorded in published collections such as Milo Rigaud's Vè-Vè (1974)
v77.summary: Designs traced on the temple floor in cornmeal, flour or ash by a Vodou priest or priestess to call a particular lwa, or spirit: a cross and cane for Legba, serpents for Damballa, a heart for Ezili. Each is made to be danced over and erased. Their origins in Kongo and Fon sign-traditions are still being traced.

v33.title: The Kartarpur Bir
v33.held: The Sodhi family, Kartarpur (Jalandhar district), Punjab
v33.summary: The volume that Sikh tradition holds is the first Adi Granth, compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 with Bhai Gurdas as scribe. It was kept by a rival claimant to the Guruship, and scholars have seldom been allowed to see it. Its authority is revered, and its text history is debated.

v69.title: The Kumulipo
v69.dated: Composed in the 18th century for the chief Kalaninuiamamao; first printed 1889
v69.held: Printed for King Kalākaua in 1889; Queen Liliʻuokalani's English translation published in 1897
v69.summary: A Hawaiian creation chant of 2,102 lines in sixteen ages, from the first night and the birth of the coral polyp to the gods and the chiefs. Composed in honour of an 18th-century chief, printed by King Kalākaua in 1889, and translated by the deposed Queen Liliʻuokalani while she was held prisoner.

olodumare.desc: The distant high god of Yoruba religion, owner of the heavens, approached through the orishas rather than worshipped directly.
